items.q: What is Thread, and how does it differ from Zigbee?
options: Thread is a wired protocol; Zigbee is wireless
Thread is a low-power IPv6 mesh on 802.15.4 — devices are natively IP-addressable (no translating hub), unlike Zigbee
items.explain: Thread uses the same 802.15.4 radio as Zigbee but makes every device natively IPv6-addressable (via 6LoWPAN), so no protocol-translating gateway is needed — it reaches the LAN via a Thread Border Router.

options: An application-layer interoperability standard (over IP) letting devices work across Apple/Google/Amazon/Samsung ecosystems
items.explain: Matter is an application-layer standard defining a common device model so smart-home devices interoperate across ecosystems. It runs over IP — on Thread, Wi-Fi, or Ethernet.

items.q: How do Matter and Thread relate?
options: They are competitors solving the same problem
Complementary layers: Matter is the application 'language'; Thread (or Wi-Fi/Ethernet) is a transport that carries it
Matter is the radio; Thread is the app layer
items.explain: They are complementary: Thread is networking (low-power IPv6 mesh); Matter is the application-layer standard (common device model). A Matter device can run over Thread OR Wi-Fi/Ethernet. 'Matter = language, Thread = road.'

items.q: A Thread network connects to the wider home LAN/internet through a:
items.explain: A Thread Border Router (often built into smart speakers/hubs) bridges the low-power Thread mesh to the home LAN/internet. Because Thread devices are natively IP, it's a bridge, not a translating gatekeeper.

items.q: Why do constrained IoT devices need lightweight cryptography instead of standard AES?
options: Standard crypto can cost too much memory, compute, and especially energy on tiny MCUs — draining batteries
Lightweight crypto is weaker but faster to break
IoT devices cannot do any encryption
items.explain: On constrained devices every CPU cycle is battery. Heavy algorithms have large footprints and high energy per operation, so lightweight crypto provides strong security at far lower resource/energy cost.

options: The algorithm NIST selected (2023) as the lightweight cryptography standard, providing authenticated encryption (AEAD) + hashing
A heavier replacement for AES on servers
items.explain: ASCON was chosen by NIST in 2023 as the lightweight crypto standard for constrained devices, offering AEAD (authenticated encryption) and hashing in a compact, efficient design.

items.q: How does ASCON differ from AES for IoT?
options: ASCON has a smaller footprint and lower energy cost on tiny MCUs (same security strength, better fit) and is AEAD by design
items.explain: ASCON is 'lightweight' in resource cost, not security strength — smaller gates/RAM/code and lower energy on constrained MCUs, with built-in authenticated encryption. AES remains excellent on powerful (often hardware-accelerated) devices.

items.q: What does 'lightweight' mean in lightweight cryptography?
options: Weaker security that is easier to break
Light in resource cost (memory, compute, energy) — NOT light in security strength
items.explain: Lightweight = resource-light, not security-light. ASCON was selected through a rigorous multi-year NIST process for both security and efficiency. (Don't confuse it with rolling your own weak cipher.)

items.q: Placing IoT devices behind a gateway/NAT improves security mainly by:
options: Making devices unreachable from the internet (no public ports), so internet-wide scanners like Shodan can't find them
items.explain: Behind NAT, devices have private, non-routable IPs and initiate only outbound connections, so internet scanners can't directly reach them — 'you can't attack what you can't see.' The gateway is a shield as well as a translator.

items.q: Using non-standard ports to hide a service is an example of:
options: Security through obscurity — a thin layer that stops automated default-port scans but NOT a determined attacker
items.explain: Non-standard ports are security through obscurity: useful against opportunistic/automated scanning, but a determined attacker scans all ports. It is never a substitute for authentication and encryption.

items.q: What is the correct role of network obfuscation in a security strategy?
options: It is the primary and only defense needed
It is one outer layer in defense-in-depth — it lowers attack noise but must be backed by authentication and encryption
It replaces the need for firewalls
items.explain: Obfuscation raises attack cost and reduces opportunistic noise but is the 'outer fence, not the vault door.' Real security still requires strong authentication, encryption, and (Unit 4) Zero Trust — relying on obscurity alone is the classic mistake.

items.q: Putting IoT devices on a separate VLAN/subnet from laptops and servers primarily provides:
options: Segmentation — containing a compromised device so it can't pivot to other systems
items.explain: Network segmentation limits the blast radius: if a weak IoT device (e.g., a bulb) is compromised, it can't reach sensitive systems — mitigating the 'one weak device endangers all' problem.
